topics.title: Probability
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: Understand the terms random, experiment, outcome, sample space, event and probability. (k, u)
Determine probabilities from experiments and real-life data. (u, s)
Differentiate between theoretical and experimental probabilities. (k, u, s)
Identify and understand mutually exclusive and independent events. (k, u)
Use probability trees to determine the probabilities of mutually exclusive and independent events. (u, s)
Use Venn diagrams to determine probabilities. (u, s, v/a)

body.text: Probability measures how likely an event is, on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment. Theoretical probability is calculated from the sample space (P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes); experimental probability comes from actually repeating a trial and recording results.

body.latex: P(\text{event}) = \frac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{total number of possible outcomes}}

body.text: Two coins are tossed. The sample space is {HH, HT, TH, TT} — 4 equally likely outcomes. The theoretical probability of getting exactly one head is 2/4 = 0.5 (HT and TH). Events are mutually exclusive if they cannot both happen at once (e.g. getting HH and getting TT on the same toss); they are independent if one happening doesn't affect the chance of the other (e.g. the two coin tosses).

A probability tree for two independent coin tosses shows each branch's probability (0.5) multiplied along the path to get the outcome's probability: P(HH) = 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25. For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(HH or TT) = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5. A Venn diagram works the same way as in Set Theory (Senior 2, Topic 13), with regions labelled by their probability instead of a count.
